title: diff-harness CRL adapter: DP-driven signer and cRLIssuer selection (brute force rejected)
description:
## What the 20 chains actually need

Checked one by one, building the adapter's checkers and recording every outcome per certificate. My earlier claim that all 20 were the reason-partitioned CRL gap was wrong: only TWO are.

  cause                                                  chains  fix belongs in
  CrlSignatureInvalid -- CRL signed by a different key       ~9  THE ADAPTER
    of the same CA (key rollover / separate CRL key)
  CrlIssuerMismatch -- indirect CRL via cRLIssuer            ~7  THE ADAPTER
  OutOfScope -- onlySomeReasons reason partitioning            2  the library
  no undetermined cert in my probe (4.5.4, 4.5.6)             2  probe artifact

## Group A: CRL signed by a different key of the same CA (~9 chains)

4.11.7, 4.12.7, 4.12.9, 4.13.19, 4.5.1, 4.6.15, 4.6.17, 4.9.6, 4.4.19

Every one reports CrlSignatureInvalid for at least one checker. PKITS classes them valid, so the CRL IS validly signed -- just not by the certificate the adapter passes as the issuer. These are the self-issued key-rollover and "Separate Certificate and CRL Keys" vectors: the CA holds several certificates and the CRL is signed by one of them while the certificate under test was signed by another. The adapter always passes chain[i+1], which is the signature-chain issuer, not necessarily the CRL signer.

pkix-revocation already solves this. CrlChecker::new_with_signer_discovery(crl_der, bundle, cert_to_check, now, verifier) takes a bundle of candidate signers and discovers which one signed the CRL. Its own documentation says it is "the right choice when the bundle is already known to be path-valid (e.g. pkix-chain already validated it)" -- which is exactly the harness's position, since it validates the path before checking revocation.

The adapter never calls it. PKITS CertPath carries the extra CA certificates; they are available and unused.

## Group B: indirect CRLs (~7 chains)

4.14.22, 4.14.24, 4.14.25, 4.14.28, 4.14.29, 4.14.30, 4.14.33

All report CrlIssuerMismatch. These are the indirectCRL and cRLIssuer vectors, where the CRL is issued by an entity other than the certificate's issuer.

pkix-revocation solves this too, via new_with_crl_issuer and with_delta_and_crl_issuer. The adapter calls neither.

Probing every CertPath certificate as a candidate cRLIssuer resolved three outright:

  4.14.22  indirectCRLCA1CRL.crl       with issuer = cert[1]
  4.14.30  indirectCRLCA4cRLIssuerCRL  with issuer = cert[2]
  4.14.33  indirectCRLCA5CRL.crl       with issuer = cert[1]

The other four did not resolve with a naive sweep. That does NOT mean they cannot: my probe held chain[i+1] as the issuer argument while varying only the cRLIssuer, and for an indirect CRL both may need to differ. Not established either way.

## Group C: the real library gap (2 chains)

4.14.18, 4.14.19 -- Valid onlySomeReasons Test18 and Test19. Both report OutOfScope.

This is the limitation a407f615 documented when it introduced it: "Combining reason-partitioned CRLs is not implemented, so valid vectors such as PKITS 4.14.18 are now out of scope rather than passed." Determining status needs several reason-partitioned CRLs combined, which pkix-revocation does not do.

Two PKITS vectors, not twenty. Still a genuine missing feature, and now correctly sized.

## Two chains I could not classify

4.5.4 and 4.5.6 produced no undetermined certificate in my probe, so my reconstruction of the chain differs from the harness's. The harness reorders PKITS CertPath bundles with pkix-path-builder because several §4.4, §4.5 and §4.14 vectors advertise CRL-signing certificates that are not in the signature chain. My probe just reversed CertPath and dropped the anchor.

That difference is itself a hint: those two likely involve exactly the extra CRL-signing certificate that path building moves, which is Group A's shape.

## What this means

Eighteen of twenty are adapter gaps of the same class as the delta-CRL pairing just fixed: the library has the capability, the harness does not use it. The pattern has now repeated three times -- single CRLs instead of base+delta, signature-chain issuer instead of discovered CRL signer, no cRLIssuer support -- so the adapter's CRL handling is simply much thinner than pkix-revocation's.

## Acceptance

[ ] Adapter uses new_with_signer_discovery with the full CertPath bundle, so a CRL signed by another of the CA's keys is found
[ ] Adapter tries cRLIssuer constructions for indirect CRLs, including with_delta_and_crl_issuer
[ ] Re-run and recount: Group A and B should mostly clear
[ ] Classify 4.5.4 and 4.5.6 against the harness's own reordered chain rather than a hand-rolled one
[ ] Decide reason-partitioned CRL combining on its real size: 2 vectors
notes:
UNBLOCKED 2026-11-25: pkix_revocation::crl_applies_to now exposes §6.3.3(b) selection, so the harness does not have to restate it. But a finding from building it changes the plan.

## The predicate is public now

crl_applies_to(cert, crl_der) -> Result<()>. It shares its implementation with check_revocation rather than duplicating the matching, which was the hazard worth avoiding.

Building it answered the question the previous note left open and added one that matters more.

## FINDING: PKITS certificates carry no cRLDistributionPoints extension

Checked directly with openssl: InvalidWrongCRLTest6EE and ValidIDPwithindirectCRLTest22EE both report nothing for -ext crlDistributionPoints. PKITS supplies CRLs out of band through CRLPath, not through DP URIs in the certificates.

So the "DP-driven selection" plan this bead carried CANNOT work as written for this corpus. There are no distribution points to drive it with. check_dp_scope's own table says an absent CDP matches unless the IDP names a distribution point -- for most PKITS CRLs that is a near no-op.

That is why crl_applies_to had to add §6.3.3(b)(1) itself: for a direct CRL, the certificate's issuer must be the CRL's issuer. Without that the predicate would accept any well-formed CRL for a PKITS certificate, which is the opposite of useful. check_dp_scope is only the distribution-point half; the issuer match lives separately in check_revocation and is not reachable through it.

## What that means for the adapter

The correct selection rule for PKITS reduces mostly to the ISSUER match, not the DP match. Which the adapter already gets, via CrlChecker::new -> check_revocation -> CrlIssuerMismatch. The diagnostics in this bead show exactly that error on the Group B chains.

So selection alone will not clear the 18. Group A (CrlSignatureInvalid, ~9 chains) is not a selection problem at all: the CRL IS the right one by issuer DN, and the adapter fails because it hands check_revocation the signature-chain issuer rather than the certificate that signed the CRL. Group B (CrlIssuerMismatch, ~7) needs the indirect path, where the DP genuinely matters -- and those certificates have no DP to name a cRLIssuer with.

That last point is worth sitting with. If a PKITS certificate has no CDP, and §6.3.3(b)(2)(i) is read as requiring a distribution point to name the cRLIssuer, then an indirect CRL can never apply to it, and the Group B chains may be unfixable without taking the lenient reading. The lenient reading is what check_dp_scope implements and what crl_applies_to's tests now pin.

## Revised plan

1. Use crl_applies_to as a FILTER before constructing any checker: a CRL the certificate does not point at is never offered, whatever signer it has. That is the constraint all three rejected strategies lacked, and it is now available without restating the rules.
2. For Group A, combine that filter with signer discovery. Strategy 3 restricted discovery by subject DN and got worse, but it added capability without adding the filter -- filter first, then discover among the certificates the CRL's issuer DN admits.
3. Measure BOTH counts every time. All three rejected strategies looked fine on one.

## Open question, recorded not resolved

Whether an indirect CRL whose IDP names no distribution point should apply to a certificate with no CDP. check_dp_scope says yes; §6.3.3(b)(2)(i) can be read as no. Changing it would change every caller of check_revocation, not just this predicate, so it is pinned by a test with the question written out rather than quietly settled.

## Acceptance

[x] Checked whether pkix-revocation can expose §6.3.3 DP selection -- it can, and now does
[x] Found that PKITS certificates have no CDP, which invalidates the DP-driven plan as originally written
[ ] Use crl_applies_to as a pre-filter in the adapter, then re-measure
[ ] Decide the indirect-CRL-without-CDP reading, since Group B may depend on it
[ ] Target unchanged: clear the 18 WITHOUT regressing the 18 negative tests
close_reason:
DONE 2026-11-25. Disagreements with NIST: 35 -> 15. Twenty fixes, zero regressions.

## The sequence that worked, after three that did not

  step                                              gt disagreements
  committed baseline                                              35
  distribution-point filter alone                                 35   (exact no-op)
  + signer discovery, gated by the filter                         26
  + CRL signers path building dropped                             18   (1 regression)
  + revoked signers excluded                                      17   (0 regressions)
  + reason-partitioned CRL combining                              15

The filter measuring as a PERFECT no-op is what made the rest safe. It removes nothing -- every CRL that previously produced a verdict was already applicable -- so it purely constrains what follows. The three rejected strategies (enumeration 35 as an 18-for-18 trade, discovery alone 44, DN-restricted discovery 46) all added capability without that constraint.

Order was the whole finding. Same ingredients, opposite outcome.

## What each step was

FILTER. pkix_revocation::crl_applies_to, added for this, exposes RFC 5280 §6.3.3(b) so the harness does not restate security-relevant matching. Checkers are now built per certificate, since applicability is a property of the (certificate, CRL) pair.

DISCOVERY. Among applicable CRLs, new_with_signer_discovery finds which certificate actually signed each -- the key-rollover and separate-CRL-key case, where a CA signs its CRL with one certificate while having issued the subject from another.

DROPPED SIGNERS. Path building reduces a bundle to one chain and drops non-links, including the CA's dedicated CRL-signing certificate in several §4.4, §4.5 and §4.14 vectors. Chain::aux_certs_der carries them through. This cost nine construction-site edits, six in tests -- churn that was not worth paying while the field served no working code, which is why an earlier attempt reverted it.

REVOKED SIGNERS. Restoring those certificates broke exactly one negative test, 4.4.21, and the reason is the sharpest thing found today. It is structurally IDENTICAL to the 4.4.19 beside it -- same topology, signing certificate a sibling, empty CRL -- and NIST fails it for one reason, found by comparing serials: the CRL signer's certificate is serial 68, revoked by TrustAnchorRootCRL, where 4.4.19's is serial 66 and is not. new_with_signer_discovery enforces cRLSign per §6.3.3(f) and requires the signer to chain to self-signed, but cannot ask whether the signer is still valid -- nothing in its inputs would let it.

REASON PARTITIONS. check_revocation_with_crls implements §6.3.3's reasons_mask accumulation, closing the gap that was documented as unimplemented.

## Worth carrying forward

A LIBRARY HELPER THAT CANNOT SEE REVOCATION. new_with_signer_discovery will trust a CRL signed by a revoked certificate if the caller hands it one. The harness now filters them out, but any other caller is exposed. That deserves its own bead: either the helper should take the information it needs, or its documentation should say plainly that the caller must pre-filter.

MEASURE BOTH DIRECTIONS, EVERY TIME. Four of the six steps above looked acceptable on one count and were only settled by checking the other. The 18-for-18 trade read as progress until the regressions were counted.

Four test premises were wrong before any code was: InvalidWrongCRLTest6EE's CRL is deliberately the wrong one; the issuer check reports CrlIssuerMismatch where a distribution-point mismatch was expected; PKITS has no partitioned CRL with a revoked entry; and this crate's fixtures are issued for 2026 where the PKITS clock of 2020 yields CrlExpired. In each case the implementation was right and the test was wrong, which is worth knowing about a session's worth of confident assertions.

## What remains

Fifteen disagreements, all predating this work, catalogued per bucket in baseline-pkits-analysis.md. None is a known adapter gap.
